narrative:
The model determined that you have an 82% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is so high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Three factors drove this decision, ranked by importance. Your class ranking in your third year of law school was the strongest influence, pushing the prediction heavily toward failure. You placed in the bottom decile (1 out of 10), far below the average of roughly 6 among students who were accepted. This low ranking signaled to the model that you struggled significantly compared with your peers later in the program.

Your first-year class ranking was the next most important factor and also pulled the prediction toward failure. Ranking in the second decile placed you well below the average of 6 for accepted students, reinforcing the pattern of academic difficulty.

Your LSAT score worked in the opposite direction. At 37, it sits almost exactly at the average for accepted students and therefore nudged the model slightly toward expecting you to pass. However, this positive influence was not strong enough to overcome the much larger negative effects from your two class rankings.

Given these results, you should focus on strengthening your academic performance and consider retaking the bar exam preparation courses or seeking additional support before reapplying. Improving your class standing in future semesters could substantially change how a similar model evaluates your application. (218 words)
